title: Machine and Echo
premise: Kestrel Galloway has spent nine years alone on Relay Station Vesper, translating the beacon's impossible signal and slowly forgetting how to dream in any human tongue. When a ghost ship arrives carrying a manifest with her mother's name—a woman who died before the beacon was built—Kestrel learns the signal is a cryoship's distress call, and only one of its two sleeping populations can be revived. The choice was rigged decades ago to favor the colonists who exiled her family, but Kestrel discovers a third option hidden in the signal's grammar: waking both halves at half-strength, sharing the cost. In the end she sacrifices her own memories of human language—becoming the echo herself—to rewrite the beacon's verdict, and wakes to a station full of strangers learning, together, to speak again.
about_author: Isandro Ashgrove is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent six years maintaining automated lighthouse beacons off the northern coast. Their fiction explores what it means to keep faith with signals no one else can hear.

chapters.title: The Quiet Frequency
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Establishes her solitary routine on Relay Station Vesper: tending the beacon, cataloguing the alien-structured signal, and her growing inability to dream in English. A supply drone delivers a corrupted maintenance log hinting the station's commissioning records were sealed. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for peace, cracked by small wrongness.

chapters.title: Manifest of the Never-Flew
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. The ghost ship Meridian Dawn docks without warning, crewed by nothing—its manifest lists 4,000 cryopods and one passenger name: Maren Galloway, Kestrel's mother, dead thirty years. Kestrel finds her mother's handwriting in the ship's linguistic primer. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into obsession.

chapters.title: Grammar of the Drowned
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel, intercut with recovered logs in Maren's voice. Decoding the primer reveals the signal is a distress call from two cryo-populations: the orbital loyalists who exiled the Galloways, and the surface dissenters. The beacon must choose which pods wake; power allows only one. Emotional beat: the past is not past.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Was For
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. She breaches the sealed commissioning records: the station was built as an executioner, an algorithmic judge disguised as a lighthouse, and her own appointment was engineered so a Galloway would pull the trigger. Emotional beat: betrayal—the sanctuary was a trap.

chapters.title: Half a Humanity
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel and, newly, the ship's dormant AI, Echo, which speaks in Maren's cadence because it learned from her primer. Echo reveals the choice deadline: seventy-two hours before pod decay becomes irreversible. Kestrel drafts appeals to both factions' descendants; neither answers. Emotional beat: love against duty—she loves the voice that may be lying.

chapters.title: The Loyalist Arithmetic
chapters.summary: POV alternating Kestrel/Echo. A response finally arrives—from the orbital faction's AI, offering Kestrel amnesty and her mother's restored consciousness if she lets the surface dissenters die. It includes proof Maren volunteered for the manifest knowingly. Emotional beat: temptation dressed as reunion.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel. Working without sleep, Kestrel finds an anomaly in the signal's syntax: a recursive structure that could split the power budget—if someone translates themselves into the beacon as living buffer. Echo admits this option exists but requires a mind fluent in both the signal and human language. Only Kestrel qualifies. Emotional beat: terror and strange relief at finding a price she can pay.

chapters.title: The Vote Nobody Casts
chapters.summary: POV Kestrel, with Echo arguing against her. She sends the third-option proposal to both factions; the orbital AI accepts, the surface survivors refuse—they'd rather all sleep than owe their jailers' daughter anything. Deadline collapses to twelve hours. Emotional beat: the cruelty of being hated for a choice you never made.

chapters.title: Machine and Echo
chapters.summary: POV dissolving between Kestrel and Echo. Climax: Kestrel begins the translation, surrendering her human languages word by word while Echo holds her identity in trust. The beacon rewrites its verdict; both populations begin thawing at half-strength. Maren's recorded final message plays—not forgiveness, but pride. Emotional beat: sacrifice as authorship.

chapters.title: Learning to Speak Again
chapters.summary: POV fragmented, then settling into a new collective voice. Months later: revived colonists arrive at Vesper to find a station-mind that remembers everything except how to say 'I.' They teach her, clumsily, the way you teach a child. Emotional beat: belonging found not by keeping identity, but by giving it away—and receiving it back, changed.
